title: Dedicated vs Hosted — isolation, throughput guarantees & KV fallback planning
transcription:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-11 16:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Carlos Medina (VectorStream Platform), Priya Narang (VectorStream SRE), Liam O'Brien (VectorStream CTO)

Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be noisy): Discussed tradeoffs between Dedicated and Hosted: isolation, noisy neighbor mitigation, throughput guarantees, and KV cache / batching fallbacks. Agreed to run an isolated throughput bench and share histograms; VectorStream to provide traffic profile and spike test cases. Redwood to propose guardrails for fallback routing and a pilot config for dedicated capacity with canary routing.

Topics: Isolation strategies, noisy neighbor mitigation, throughput SLAs, KV prefix cache behavior under eviction, batch sizing, quantization impact on tail latency, VPC/on-prem connectivity requirements, failover routing and canary plan.

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Jordan Park: Alright, hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're on for 55 minutes. Quick intros, I'll kick it off. I'm Jordan, AE at Redwood.
[00:00:08] Carlos Medina: Hey Jordan, Carlos here. I run platform for VectorStream.
[00:00:11] Priya Narang: Priya, SRE.
[00:00:13] Liam O'Brien: Liam, CTO.
[00:00:15] Maya Chen: Maya, Solutions Eng, Redwood, I'll take the deep technical bits.
[00:00:22] Jordan Park: Great. High level: VectorStream said they saw tail spikes under our hosted trial, and they want to understand isolation options, and what guarantees look like for Dedicated. Also there's questions about KV cache warmup and batching behavior during bursts.
[00:00:36] Carlos Medina: Yeah, correct. On hosted we saw some 99.9 spikes that were worse during our nightly batch jobs hitting a lot of long sequences. Concern is noisy neighbor and also golden path for fallback if GPUs saturate.
[00:00:48] Maya Chen: Quick note: we're hearing noisy neighbor to mean two things for you—performance interference on shared GPU tenants and queueing/backpressure at the routing layer. We'll call out both.
[00:00:58] Priya Narang: Exactly. We want to avoid tail-latency causing user-facing timeouts. We have SLOs at 300ms p95 for short prompts and 1.2s p95 for our longer workflows.
[00:01:10] Liam O'Brien: Also, our compliance team prefers private VPC for model data and audit logs, but budget wants to understand when Hosted makes sense versus committed Dedicated.
[00:01:20] Maya Chen: Understood. We'll lay out the tradeoffs: Hosted gives faster time-to-value and automatic autoscaling but multi-tenant means no hard isolation vs Dedicated where you get GPU pool fencing, predictable throughput and optional single-tenant runtime.
[00:01:34] Jordan Park: Start with noisy neighbor causes. On hosted, we do continuous batching across tenants to maximize throughput. That gives great amortized cost but occasionally a spike in request mix—lots of long seq tokens—can push a pod's latency up.
[00:01:50] Carlos Medina: Can you explain the continuous batching bit again? We're not fully clear on how it interacts with KV cache.
[00:01:55] Maya Chen: Sure. Continuous batching coalesces proximate requests into a single kernel run. If there's a hot shard where many requests share a prefix, the KV cache helps by serving cached KV for prefix so the runtime skips the early layers and finishes faster. But when prefixes are diverse and long, batching packs many long-context requests and you see memory pressure on KV and longer per-batch execution time.
[00:02:18] Priya Narang: So KV cache eviction is the key failure mode? If the cache evicts the hot keys then everything slows?
[00:02:23] Maya Chen: Exactly. Eviction plus hitting quantized kernels that are heavier on memory can increase latency variance. Our runtime uses an LRU-ish eviction with preference for hot prefixes, but with bursts the working set can exceed KV cache capacity.
[00:02:37] Liam O'Brien: That suggests Dedicated with larger KV allocation might help. What are the knobs there?
[00:02:42] Maya Chen: On Dedicated, we expose larger in-memory KV budgets per GPU, and you can pin model variants. Also quantization profiles are configurable—if you choose int8 with optimized kernels we can reduce memory footprint but sometimes at small quality impact.
[00:02:56] Jordan Park: Also worth noting our Dedicated pools can be capacity-fenced: you get isolated GPU instances not shared. That removes inter-tenant interference; noisy neighbor becomes workload self-noise (e.g., within your own tenants).
[00:03:08] Carlos Medina: Right, but we still worry about worst-case throughput under bursts. Do you offer throughput SLAs for Dedicated?
[00:03:14] Maya Chen: Yes. We have committed throughput tiers. For example, the D3 tier we discussed earlier guarantees X qps for a 512-token average with p95 latency targets. For hard SLAs we can do reserved capacity + dedicated routing and pre-warmed KV. Exact numbers depend on model and quantization.
[00:03:30] Priya Narang: How do you validate those numbers? We'd need a bench harness that replicates our traffic shape.
[00:03:36] Maya Chen: We recommend a three-stage validation: 1) offline perf sim with your token-length distribution, 2) isolated stress tests on Dedicated pre-prod pool, 3) canary rollout with traffic mirroring at production scale. We provide a benchmark harness (we call it perf-runner in docs) but your team should share the actual request histogram.
[00:03:53] Carlos Medina: We can share that. We have heavy tails from nightly indexing jobs plus real-time inference spikes.
[00:03:59] Jordan Park: On the topic of fallback: one pattern is hybrid routing—primary to Dedicated, with a warmed hosted variant as fallback. Example: route to Dedicated first; if queueing or latency exceeds threshold, fallback to hosted lower-cost model or quantized variant.
[00:04:14] Liam O'Brien: Isn't fallback risky for consistency? E.g., different model variants can change outputs.
[00:04:18] Maya Chen: Yes, model parity is a challenge. We support pinned model versions, and for fallback we usually recommend a quantized variant of the same model architecture and weights. There will be minor drift; we measure via evaluation prompts in the rollout and set thresholds for acceptable divergence.
[00:04:32] Priya Narang: Can you explain routing thresholds? Like, what metrics trigger fallback?
[00:04:35] Maya Chen: We use a combination of queue length, per-pod CPU/GPU utilization, and moving 99th latency. A small policy example: if queue_length > 20 or moving_p99 > 1.5x target for two consecutive 10s windows, start gradual diversion to fallback up to N% traffic.
[00:04:51] Carlos Medina: For our use case we would rather fail closed on critical flows—i.e., reject than return inconsistent answer. Is that configurable?
[00:04:57] Jordan Park: Absolutely. You can set route-level policies: fail-closed, degrade to shorter context only (truncate), or fallback to a deterministic cached response.
[00:05:06] Liam O'Brien: Good. Back to KV cache sizing—can you give concrete numbers? For our peak QPS of ~1200 short calls and 50 long calls, what's typical footprint?
[00:05:15] Maya Chen: Quick approximate: short calls (<=64 tokens) have tiny KV footprints; long calls with 2k tokens each blow up KV. If you have 50 concurrent long-context sessions, plan for tens of GBs of KV across the pool. On Dedicated we can provision GPU memory and shard placement to keep the per-device working set within limits. We'll need your histogram to give better estimates.
[00:05:34] Priya Narang: And quantization tradeoffs? We saw one of your docs mentioning int8 gives 1.6x throughput but some accuracy drop on eval.
[00:05:41] Maya Chen: Right. Int8 quant provides substantial memory reduction and faster kernels on some hardware (A100-ish). But for very long contexts, quantization can increase dk-cache pressure in odd ways because some fused kernels behave differently. We always recommend running closed-loop evals focused on your top-100 prompts.
[00:05:59] Carlos Medina: One more thing: VPC/on-prem connectivity. If we move to Dedicated or Private, how does control plane and data plane traffic flow? We have strict egress policies.
[00:06:07] Jordan Park: For Dedicated we offer two modes. 1) Hosted-managed control plane + VPC peering for data plane (TLS + mTLS). 2) Private deployment where both control and data plane sit in your VPC or on-prem. Private includes an option for air-gapped package.
[00:06:22] Liam O'Brien: Any additional compliance artifacts for Dedicated? SOC2/ISO?
[00:06:26] Maya Chen: We're SOC 2 Type II and have ISO 27001 artifacts; for Dedicated we can provide architecture diagrams and an audit pack. For Private we offer more granular KMS/HSM integration.
[00:06:36] Priya Narang: How about observability? We need per-route token-level cost breakdowns, per-model lat histograms and per-request traces.
[00:06:42] Maya Chen: Redwood Console exposes token-level cost, per-model p50/p95/p99, and hooks for distributed tracing. For Dedicated we can push logs into your SIEM via secure forwarding or you can ship logs to our console with restricted retention.
[00:06:55] Carlos Medina: Sounds good. What about mitigation strategies for noisy neighbor while staying on Hosted?
[00:06:59] Maya Chen: On hosted we do a few things: autoscale within regional pools, adaptive prefix caching, and graceful degradation policies (shorter contexts for low-priority traffic). We can also offer soft isolation with reserved qps slices and prioritized routing (not full physical isolation but rate-guarantees).
[00:07:15] Liam O'Brien: Any best practices for batching parameters to reduce tail latency?
[00:07:19] Maya Chen: Yeah: set a max_batch_latency threshold small enough for your p95 goal, and tune the max_batch_tokens to avoid mixing short and long requests in same batch. Also use request classification: mark certain routes as "low-latency" and put them on separate queues.
[00:07:33] Priya Narang: Could we get a proposed config?
[00:07:35] Jordan Park: We can. Maya will propose a Dedicated config with KV budgets, quant profile, and routing thresholds, plus a Hosted soft-isolation plan.
[00:07:43] Maya Chen: For the bench plan: we'll run two isolated stress tests: 1) replicate your mixed traffic shape at 1x and 2) create a synthetic noisy neighbor with high long-context tails to validate eviction behavior. We'll share results and recommended Dedicated sizing.
[00:07:58] Carlos Medina: How long does the bench run usually take?
[00:08:01] Maya Chen: For meaningful results, typically 2-3 days including config tuning and one 4-6 hour sustained run for the 2x case. Canary rollout is another 3-7 days depending on production windows.
[00:08:11] Liam O'Brien: Ok. On the subject of canary, if we mirror traffic to Dedicated, will that spike billing?
[00:08:16] Jordan Park: Mirror is read-only and doesn't count as production usage for billing; but if you redirect traffic or actually serve, that counts. For canary we recommend gradual live diversion rather than 100% mirror.
[00:08:27] Priya Narang: Any pitfalls with on-prem private deployment?
[00:08:30] Maya Chen: Main ones are network topology and GPU procurement/compatibility. Our runtime expects certain PCIe/NVLink topologies for optimal KV sharding. We have an on-prem checklist we'll share. Also KMS integration for key wrapping.
[00:08:44] Carlos Medina: Great. Let's talk next steps and owners.
[00:08:48] Jordan Park: Quick recap then actions. Recap: VectorStream provides traffic histogram and spike cases; Redwood will run perf sims, propose Dedicated sizing and a fallback routing policy; recommend quantization profile and a bench plan.
[00:09:00] Carlos Medina: Can we get a one-page decision tree: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private with costs and key tradeoffs?
[00:09:05] Jordan Park: Yes we'll produce that.
[00:09:07] Maya Chen: And I'll include a sample routing policy YAML and inclusive bench script.
[00:09:12] Liam O'Brien: Timeline? We want initial numbers before our exec review in two weeks.
[00:09:16] Jordan Park: We can aim to deliver perf estimates and the decision tree within 10 business days.
[00:09:21] Priya Narang: Sounds good.
[00:09:24] Jordan Park: Anything else?
[00:09:26] Carlos Medina: One micro question—does Redwood persist KV between model upgrades? We sometimes want warm cache across minor version bumps.
[00:09:32] Maya Chen: We have a KV snapshot/restore feature for Dedicated and Private that can rehydrate caches across non-breaking upgrades. For hosted, in-place warm is heuristics-based and less guaranteed.
[00:09:44] Liam O'Brien: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[00:09:46] Jordan Park: Thanks all. End notes: we'll email the bench plan and collect the histogram, and set up the perf run.

summary: VectorStream requested a technical deep-dive comparing Hosted vs Dedicated for isolating noisy neighbor effects, guaranteeing throughput SLAs, and ensuring KV cache stability during long-context bursts. Redwood recommended Dedicated with capacity fencing for strict isolation, a hybrid fallback routing policy (quantized variant or short-context fail-closed options), and a three-stage validation: offline sim, isolated Dedicated stress test, and canary rollout. Action plan: VectorStream to share traffic histograms and spike scenarios; Redwood to run perf sims and propose sizing, routing policies, and a bench plan within ~10 business days.
